nb01_zero_context.content:
# Internet Access and Economic Development in Rwanda and Kenya

I can't access live databases, so the figures below come from my training data. They are approximate and may be outdated, and definitions differ across sources (for example, subscriptions versus unique users). Check the latest releases before citing numbers in formal work.

## Snapshot comparison (approximate, ~2022–2024)

| Indicator | Kenya | Rwanda |
|---|---|---|
| Population | ~55 million | ~14 million |
| GDP (current US$) | ~$110–115 billion | ~$13–14 billion |
| GDP per capita | ~$2,000–2,200 | ~$950–1,050 |
| Real GDP growth | ~5% (2023), ~4–5% (2024) | ~8% (2023), ~9–10% (2024) |
| Internet users (share of population) | roughly 40% | roughly 30–40% (estimates vary widely) |
| Mobile broadband | Large base of mobile data subscriptions, widely used | Expanding; 4G population coverage is high |
| Mobile money | Very high adoption (M-Pesa is a global reference case) | High adoption, growing via national platforms |
| Human Development Index | ~0.58 (mid-tier) | ~0.53 (low-medium tier, improving) |
| Poverty | ~36% national poverty line (2020 survey) | Fell from ~77% (2001) to ~38% (2016/17); further decline reported in later surveys |

## Main patterns

**1. Both countries have expanded access quickly, mostly through mobile.** Mobile phones, not fixed broadband, drive connectivity in both. Fixed broadband and household internet access remain low, especially outside cities.

**2. Kenya's model is market-led and mobile-money-driven.** Competition among mobile operators, a dense private sector, and M-Pesa have made Kenya a reference case for mobile-enabled finance and digital services. Its growth has been broad-based, though poverty and inequality remain high.

**3. Rwanda's model is state-led and infrastructure-focused.** The government built a national fiber backbone, pursued universal coverage targets, and promoted digital services through institutions such as Smart Rwanda and the Kigali Innovation City initiative. Its growth has been faster, but from a lower income base.

**4. Affordability is a binding constraint in both countries.** Data prices relative to income remain high for many households, so access does not automatically translate into use. Usage gaps are largest among women, rural residents, and low-income groups.

**5. Connectivity and growth move together, though causality is hard to isolate.** Cross-country studies consistently link broadband and mobile adoption to productivity and GDP growth, and both countries' digital strategies assume this relationship. Disentangling the effect of internet access from other reforms in these two countries requires careful econometric work.

## Suggested sources

- **ITU**, *Facts and Figures* (2024) and *Measuring Digital Development: Facts and Figures* (ITU DataHub): internet use and affordability indicators.
- **World Bank**, World Development Indicators (databank.worldbank.org): GDP, GDP per capita, poverty, and growth.
- **IMF**, *World Economic Outlook* (October 2024 edition): growth forecasts and country data.
- **Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS)**, *Economic Survey 2024* and *Kenya Poverty Report*.
- **Communications Authority of Kenya**, *Quarterly Sector Statistics Reports*: mobile and internet subscriptions. Note that these count subscriptions, not individuals.
- **Rwanda Utilities Regulatory Authority (RURA)**, annual reports and ICT sector statistics.
- **National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda (NISR)**, *Integrated Household Living Conditions Survey (EICV)* and ICT household surveys: poverty and household internet access.
- **Smart Rwanda Master Plan 2050** and related Rwandan ICT strategy documents.
- **GSMA**, *The Mobile Economy Sub-Saharan Africa* (annual): mobile connectivity and economic contribution.
- **Alliance for Affordable Internet (A4AI)**, *Affordability Report*: data-price comparisons.
- **DataReportal** (*Digital 2024/2025* country reports): internet user estimates.
- **UNDP**, *Human Development Report*: HDI values.

If you tell me which years or indicators matter most for your purpose, I can narrow the comparison and suggest the most appropriate source for each figure.

nb01_with_context.content:
## Internet access and economic development in Kenya and Rwanda, 2010 to 2024

**Latest comparison (2024):**

| Indicator | Kenya | Rwanda |
|---|---|---|
| Internet use (% of population) | 35.0 [kenya-digital] | 31.7 [rwanda-digital] |
| Mobile subscriptions (per 100 people) | 126.5 [kenya-digital] | 93.2 [rwanda-digital] |
| GDP per capita (current US$) | 2,133 [kenya-economy] | 1,060 [rwanda-economy] |
| Real GDP growth | 4.7% [kenya-economy] | 7.2% [rwanda-economy] |
| Population | 56.4 million [kenya-digital] | 14.3 million [rwanda-digital] |

**Internet use.** Both countries have grown quickly from low bases. Kenya rose from 7.2% in 2010 to 35.0% in 2024 [kenya-digital]. Rwanda rose from 8.0% to 31.7% over the same period [rwanda-digital]. Kenya's share more than doubled between 2010 and 2015 [kenya-digital], while Rwanda's nearly doubled between 2015 and 2020 [rwanda-digital]. Kenya leads in 2024, but the gap is small.

**Mobile subscriptions.** Rwanda started lower, at 34.4 per 100 people in 2010 [rwanda-digital], compared with 60.0 in Kenya [kenya-digital]. Kenya's figure passed 100 around 2020 (117.6) [kenya-digital], and Rwanda's stayed below 100 throughout [rwanda-digital]. The source notes that values above 100 reflect multiple subscriptions per person and inactive SIM cards, so they do not show what share of people own a phone [kenya-digital].

**Economic development.** Kenya's GDP per capita is roughly double Rwanda's in 2024: 2,133 against 1,060 [kenya-economy; rwanda-economy]. Rwanda's rose by about 80% between 2010 and 2024 from a lower starting point (587 to 1,060) [rwanda-economy]. Kenya's roughly doubled from 1,092 to 2,133 [kenya-economy]. Both series are in current dollars, so exchange rates and prices affect them as well as real output. Kenya's 2023 decline coincides with a shilling depreciation [kenya-economy].

**Growth.** Rwanda has grown faster recently: 9.8% in 2022, 8.6% in 2023, and 7.2% in 2024 [rwanda-economy]. Kenya recorded 4.9%, 5.7%, and 4.7% over the same years [kenya-economy]. Both economies contracted in 2020, Kenya by 0.3% [kenya-economy] and Rwanda by 2.8% [rwanda-economy].

**Main patterns:**
- Internet use roughly tripled or quadrupled in both countries between 2010 and 2024 but remains around a third of the population.
- Mobile subscriptions have grown faster than internet use. Kenya's subscriptions exceed one per person, while internet use is still about a third of the population [kenya-digital].
- Kenya has the higher income level, while Rwanda has recently grown faster.

**Limitations.** The context does not analyse causal links between connectivity and income, so it cannot show whether internet access drives growth or the reverse. The Rwanda document states that growth exceeded 7% in 10 of 15 years [rwanda-economy], but it gives values for only six years, so I could not verify that count. Similarly, the Kenya document's statement that its economy grew in every year except 2020 [kenya-economy] is not checkable against the years it lists.

nb01_ambiguous_no_instruction.content:
Kenya is **partly connected**. Internet use reaches a little over a third of the population, while mobile subscriptions are numerous enough to exceed the population.

- **Internet use:** 35.0% of people in 2024, up from 7.2% in 2010. That leaves roughly two-thirds of Kenyans (about 37 million of 56.4 million) not using the internet.
- **Mobile subscriptions:** 126.5 per 100 people in 2024. This is a count of subscriptions, not people. Many individuals hold multiple SIM cards, and some cards are inactive, so this figure does not show how many people have a phone.
- **Growth:** The share of internet users has risen steadily. The context says the fastest absolute growth was in 2010–2015, but the data suggest otherwise. Internet use rose about 9.4 points in 2010–2015, but about 10.3 points in just four years, 2020–2024. The recent pace is therefore the fastest.

Overall, mobile access is widespread, but regular internet use is still limited to about a third of the population. The gap between the two indicators suggests that cost of data and devices, not basic network access, may be the main constraint.

## Internet access and economic development in Rwanda and Kenya

**Economic development: not covered.** The passages contain no GDP, income, poverty, or other economic indicators for either country, so I can't assess how economic development has changed. The discussion below covers internet access and mobile subscriptions only.

### Internet use, latest available data

- **Rwanda:** 31.7% of the population in 2024, up from 8.0% in 2010 [rwanda-digital · Internet use · 2026].
- **Kenya:** 35.0% of the population in 2024, up from 7.2% in 2010 [kenya-digital · Internet use · 2026].

### Main patterns

- **Both countries grew substantially.** Rwanda gained about 24 percentage points and Kenya about 28 over 2010–2024 [rwanda-digital · Internet use · 2026; kenya-digital · Internet use · 2026].
- **Rwanda's fastest growth was 2015–2020,** when its share nearly doubled, from 12.5% to 23.8%. Growth then slowed to 2023 and picked up in 2024 [rwanda-digital · Internet use · 2026].
- **Kenya's fastest growth was 2010–2015,** when its share more than doubled, from 7.2% to 16.6%. Growth continued after 2020, reaching 24.7% in 2020, 29.4% in 2022, 32.1% in 2023, and 35.0% in 2024 [kenya-digital · Internet use · 2026].
- **Kenya led in every year where both countries have figures.** The gap was 4.1 points in 2015 (16.6% vs 12.5%) and narrowed to 0.9 points in 2020 (24.7% vs 23.8%). It widened again to 3.3 points in 2024 (35.0% vs 31.7%) [regional-2016 · intro · 2016; rwanda-digital · Internet use · 2026; kenya-digital · Internet use · 2026].
- **Mobile subscriptions were high in both countries in 2015:** 80.1 per 100 people in Kenya and 75.3 per 100 in Rwanda. No later figures are given [regional-2016 · intro · 2016].

### Caveats

- The 2016 regional summary projected that internet use would reach about 25% by 2020 and about half the population by 2025 [regional-2016 · intro · 2016]. The 2020 figures came close (23.8% for Rwanda, 24.7% for Kenya). The 2025 projection cannot be checked against the supplied data, and the 2024 values sit well below half. That summary also says later values would be added as released, so its figures are superseded by the 2026 country notes.
- The mobile money note gives no figures. It says mobile money use is not the same as internet use, since the service works through USSD on basic phones [mobile-money · intro · 2026]. It also describes Rwanda's services as having grown later and faster than Kenya's, but supplies no indicator values to support that comparison [mobile-money · intro · 2026].

The 2020 actuals were close to that projection: 24.7% in Kenya and 23.8% in Rwanda [kenya-digital · Internet use · 2026; rwanda-digital · Internet use · 2026]. The passages do not include a 2025 figure, so the half-population projection cannot be checked.

**GDP per capita** (current US dollars)

- **Rwanda** rose from 587 in 2010 to 726 in 2015, 803 in 2020, 1,007 in 2022, 1,061 in 2023, and 1,060 in 2024 [rwanda-economy · GDP per capita · 2026]. It passed 1,000 in 2022. - **Kenya** rose from 1,092 in 2010 to 1,489 in 2015, 1,928 in 2020, 2,110 in 2022, 1,943 in 2023, and 2,133 in 2024 [kenya-economy · GDP per capita · 2026]. GDP per capita roughly doubled over the period. Kenya's economy grew in every year except 2020 [kenya-economy · Reading the two indicators together · 2026].
- Kenya's GDP per capita was higher than Rwanda's throughout the period, with the gap widening from about 500 dollars in 2010 to about 1,070 dollars in 2024 (calculated from the figures above).

**Main patterns**

1. Internet use grew in both countries. Kenya had the larger gain and the higher 2024 share, and both countries grew fastest in the early part of the period. Rwanda's fastest growth came between 2015 and 2020 [rwanda-digital · Internet use · 2026; kenya-digital · Internet use · 2026].
2. Both economies grew over the period, with a shared dip in 2020. Rwanda's per-capita figure stalled after 2023, and Kenya's fell in 2023 [rwanda-economy · GDP per capita · 2026; kenya-economy · GDP per capita · 2026].
3. The GDP series are in current dollars, so exchange rates and prices affect them as well as real output. The 2023 decline in Kenya coincides with a depreciation of the shilling [kenya-economy · GDP per capita · 2026]. The same caveat applies to Rwanda's series [rwanda-economy · GDP per capita · 2026].

**Limitations**

- The passages show that internet use and GDP per capita rose together over the period, but they do not establish a causal link between them.
- The passages contain no mobile money figures. The mobile money note states that account indicators are published in the Global Findex database and in national financial-inclusion surveys [mobile-money · intro · 2026].

nb06_tools_q7.content:
The indicator is **"Individuals using the Internet (% of population)."** It counts people who have used the internet from any location in the last three months, divided by the total population. Use on any device counts, including a computer, mobile phone, games console, or digital TV. It is a share of people, not of connections or subscriptions. Mobile subscriptions and fixed broadband figures measure different things and can't be substituted for it. Subscriptions can exceed the population count, and broadband connections are shared within households.

When comparing years, keep these points in mind:

- **Survey and estimate values can sit in the same series.** The ITU marks which method it used in its own database, but the World Development Indicators carry the value without that mark. Check the source before assuming two years were measured the same way.
- **Survey changes can create breaks.** A large jump between two years may reflect a change in survey design rather than a real change in use. Look for methodology notes before reading a jump as growth.
- **The three-month reference period counts occasional use.** The indicator says nothing about how often people go online, how fast their connection is, or what it costs.
- **The denominator is the whole population, including children.** Shares among adults will be higher, so don't compare these figures with adult-only surveys.

I haven't pulled any values yet. If you tell me which country and years you want, I can retrieve the series and show how it changes over time.
